title: SIMKHAI || HotWax Commerce
summary:
The meeting reviewed HotWax Commerce inventory workflows, including transfer-order receiving and fulfillment, customer-order fulfillment, cycle counting, and pricing. The demonstrations covered integrations with NetSuite and Shopify, discrepancy handling, tracking, partial shipments, inventory adjustments, and reporting.

Transfer-order receiving supports shared transfer numbers, tracking-code scanning, partial receipts, over-receipts, unexpected items, and real-time Shopify inventory updates. NetSuite item-fulfillment numbers are stored and could be surfaced in HotWax to help stores match shipments to box labels. Store-reported discrepancies are accepted as counted, with the transfer order closed in NetSuite and inventory adjusted. Discrepancy units are currently removed from inventory rather than automatically returned to the source warehouse. RFID is supported, although a full retailer supply-chain implementation has not yet been completed.

Transfer-order fulfillment supports partial shipments, carrier-label generation, tracking codes, pick tickets, and store-created transfers. Stores can close unfulfilled quantities, canceling the remaining request in NetSuite while preserving existing store inventory for later cycle counting. Customer-order fulfillment includes pick waves, shipping-priority filters, multiple packages, rejection reasons, automatic rerouting, and configurable carrier accounts by source location.

Cycle counting supports assigned counts, concurrent sessions, scanner-optimized workflows, hard, directed, and dynamic counts, manager review, compliance filters, bulk damage adjustments, and variance approval or rejection. Accepted variances synchronize to NetSuite as item adjustments and to Shopify, with exportable count data. Inventory adjustments can be reconciled through an internal identifier containing the HotWax ID. Filtering variances by price point is not currently available; cost-of-goods and percentage thresholds can prioritize higher-value discrepancies, and retail price may be added to exports if required.

Pricing was reduced to $750 per month for volumes exceeding 2,500 orders, with no planned increase at that volume. The proposal also includes a $1,000 one-time implementation fee and a $10,000 one-time customization fee for try-and-buy or consignment functionality. The monthly pricing covers the demonstrated modules, including online channels, pre-orders, retail receiving, and cycle counting. Scaled pricing remains dependent on projected Shopify order volume and is based on order count rather than revenue.

topics: HotWax supports store-friendly transfer-order receiving without requiring store teams to operate in NetSuite.
Stores can receive transfer orders in partial sessions, with each session saved as an item receipt in NetSuite.
Receiving discrepancies respect the store count, close the transfer order, adjust inventory, and generate reporting for operational analysis.
Discrepancy units are currently adjusted out of inventory rather than automatically restocked at the source warehouse.
HotWax supports over-receiving and unexpected items through scanning, with those events included in discrepancy reporting.
RFID is supported, but no retailer has yet completed a full supply-chain RFID implementation with HotWax.
Transfer-order fulfillment supports partial quantities, integrated shipping-label generation, tracking codes, and printable pick tickets.
Closing unfulfilled transfer-order quantities cancels the remaining shipping request in NetSuite while leaving current store inventory unchanged.
Customer-order fulfillment includes pick waves, shipping-priority filters, rejection reasons, and automatic rerouting through the OMS.
Cycle counts support hard, directed, and dynamic counting workflows with manager approval and NetSuite and Shopify synchronization.
Inventory adjustments can be reconciled across systems using the internal identifier and HotWax ID.
Cost-of-goods filtering and percentage thresholds can help identify financially significant inventory variances when price-point filtering is unavailable.
The proposed recurring price is $750 per month, with a $1,000 one-time onboarding fee.
Try-and-buy or consignment customization carries a separate one-time fee of $10,000.
The quoted pricing covers the reviewed modules, including online channels, pre-orders, retail receiving, and cycle counts.
Martin will provide projected Shopify order volumes so pricing can be evaluated as the business scales.
Pricing projections should use order counts rather than revenue because the commercial model is based on a per-order fee.
